details:
**Ushuaia**
The largest city of Tierra del Fuego and capital of Argentina's Tierra del Fuego Province. Lying on the Beagle Channel, it is generally considered the southernmost city in the world, and many tourist cruises to Antarctica depart from it. Its name comes from the Yaghan language.

**Strait of Magellan**
The sea passage that separates Tierra del Fuego from the South American mainland and the rest of Patagonia. Ferdinand Magellan sailed through it in 1520 and is credited with naming the islands "Land of Fire" after the many native campfires he saw along the shore.

**"Land of Fire"**
The English translation of Tierra del Fuego, an archipelago at the southern tip of South America that is divided between Argentina (eastern part) and Chile (western part). Its main island is called Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego.

**Mount Darwin (Monte Darwin)**
One of the highest peaks of the archipelago, in the Cordillera Darwin of the Chilean section. It was named for Charles Darwin, who visited the region during the survey voyage of the HMS Beagle. Monte Sarmiento is another major peak of the range.

**Yaghan (Yagan) people and language**
An indigenous seafaring people of the region's southern islands. Their language is famous as the source of "mamihlapinatapai," often called the most untranslatable word (a look shared by two people who each wish the other would act first). Its last native speaker, Cristina Calderón, died in 2022.

**Navarino Island and Puerto Williams**
A Chilean island south of the Beagle Channel. It holds the town of Puerto Williams, one of the world's southernmost settlements, as well as Yaghan middens and a museum of Yaghan culture.

**Selk'nam (Ona) genocide**
The Selk'nam, also called the Ona, were the main indigenous people of the large island. They were massacred in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by gold prospectors and sheep ranchers, and many survivors were relocated to a Salesian mission on Dawson Island. Other native groups include the Haush and the Alacaluf (Kawésqar).

**Julius Popper and the gold rush**
A Romanian-born engineer and adventurer who led a gold rush in Tierra del Fuego that began in the 1880s. He is notorious for his role in killing the Selk'nam, and the rush brought many Croatian immigrants who settled towns such as Porvenir in the Chilean section.

**Beagle Channel**
A strait along the southern coast of the main island, named after HMS Beagle. Ushuaia lies on it. Argentina and Chile disputed the Picton, Lennox, and Nueva Islands at its eastern end in the Beagle conflict, which nearly led to war in 1978 and was settled through papal mediation in 1984.

**Invasive beavers**
North American beavers were introduced in 1946 to start a fur trade. With no natural predators, they spread widely and destroyed forests, prompting a huge eradication effort described as one of the largest ever planned.

**Cape Horn**
The southernmost headland of the archipelago, on Chilean Hornos Island. It marks the northern edge of the Drake Passage, which separates South America from Antarctica.

**Robert FitzRoy and the Beagle voyages**
Captain of HMS Beagle, who surveyed the region and brought four Fuegian natives back to England on his first voyage. He returned three of them home on the second voyage, which also carried Charles Darwin.

**Isla de los Estados (Staten Island)**
An island at the eastern end of the archipelago, belonging to Argentina and named by Dutch explorers. It shares its English name with the New York borough.

**VAT exemption and electronics manufacturing**
Argentina's Tierra del Fuego Province has special tax privileges, including an exemption from value-added tax. As a result, the town of Río Grande has become a hub for assembling electronics such as laptops and phones.

**Isla Desolación and rainfall contrast**
Desolación Island lies at the rainy western end of the archipelago and receives many times more precipitation than the drier, flatter east, where steppe and oil fields are found.
